title: Potatoes for a Hangover: Mashed, Baked, or Fries? What Helps
excerpt: Are potatoes good for a hangover? What baked, mashed, and fried potatoes can and can't do the morning after, the potassium myth, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Are potatoes good for a hangover? What mashed, baked, and fried potatoes actually do the morning after, the potassium myth, and the best ways to eat them.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** potatoes are one of the better things you can eat when you're hungover, but they aren't a cure, and they don't "soak up" the alcohol that's already in your blood. What a plain potato does well is fairly simple. It gives you easy, filling carbohydrate when your blood sugar may be running low, it's bland enough to sit on a queasy stomach, and it carries a useful amount of potassium, water, and a pinch of vitamin C. How you cook it matters a lot. A baked or mashed potato is gentle. A pile of fries or a bag of chips is a different meal, and on a sore stomach it can make you feel worse. This guide explains what potatoes can and can't do the morning after, which kinds work best, and how to fit them into a realistic recovery plan.

**The quick rules:** Choose a baked, boiled, or mashed potato over fried ones if your stomach is unsettled. Add a little salt and drink water or an electrolyte drink with it. Pair it with some protein, like eggs, if you can manage it. Don't expect it to fix a headache or speed up how fast your body clears alcohol. If you've been vomiting, wait until you can keep small sips of fluid down before you try solid food.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover after a night out should be getting better by the afternoon or evening and gone within about a day. **Get medical help if** you can't keep any fluids down for many hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or worsening belly pain, you're confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, you have a seizure, your heart is racing or beating irregularly and won't settle, or you show signs of serious dehydration (very little or no urine, dizziness when you stand, a racing pulse). If someone who drank a lot can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin, that can be alcohol poisoning. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away. If you drink heavily most days and get shaky, sweaty, anxious, or start seeing or hearing things when you stop, that is alcohol withdrawal, not a hangover, and it needs a doctor, because it can become dangerous.

## Are Potatoes Good for a Hangover?

Yes, as food goes, potatoes are a good choice. They just aren't magic. Here's the realistic picture.

A hangover is not one single problem. Researchers who study it, including the group of scientists known as the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, describe it as a cluster of symptoms: headache, tiredness, nausea, poor concentration, thirst, low mood, and a general sense of feeling unwell. Several things seem to drive it at once, including the body's inflammatory response to alcohol, disrupted sleep, the effects of acetaldehyde (a toxic substance your liver makes when it breaks down alcohol), irritation of the stomach lining, and mild dehydration. No food reverses all of that.

What food can do is fix the parts that are about running on empty. That's where potatoes fit well:

- **They're easy carbohydrate.** Alcohol can push blood sugar down, especially if you drank without eating. A potato restores some of that fuel without much effort from your stomach.
- **They're bland and starchy.** Plain starchy foods are what most people can face when they feel queasy, for the same reason toast and crackers are a classic choice.
- **They bring potassium and water.** A potato is mostly water and is one of the richer everyday sources of potassium. That's helpful if you lost fluid from vomiting or diarrhea.
- **They're filling.** A real meal helps you stop grazing on whatever junk is nearby and gets you back to feeling human.

What a potato won't do is lower your blood alcohol, cure a headache on its own, or undo a poor night's sleep. Hold it to the job it can actually do and it's a solid pick.

## Why Your Body Wants Starch the Morning After

The urge to eat a mountain of carbs after drinking is not just a craving. There's some real biology behind it.

### Alcohol can drop your blood sugar

Your liver normally keeps your blood sugar steady overnight by releasing stored sugar and by making new glucose from other building blocks (a process called gluconeogenesis). Breaking down alcohol ties up the same chemical machinery the liver uses for that second job. So while you're processing a lot of alcohol, your liver is worse at keeping your blood sugar up. If you also skipped dinner, the stored sugar may already be low.

The result, for some people, is a morning of shakiness, weakness, irritability, and a foggy head that improves after eating. Researchers have not found that low blood sugar explains the whole hangover, and many hungover people have normal readings. But when it is part of the picture, carbohydrate is the direct fix, and a potato is an easy way to get it.

If you get shaky after drinking, our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains the usual causes and when shaking is a warning sign rather than just a rough morning.

### Your stomach is irritated

Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid production. That's a big part of hangover nausea and heartburn. Heavy, greasy, spicy, or very acidic food can aggravate it. Soft, plain starch tends to be the easiest thing to keep down. A plain baked or mashed potato lands in the same gentle category as rice, toast, and crackers.

### You're probably a bit dry

Alcohol makes you urinate more because it suppresses vasopressin, a hormone that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. Add a warm bar, a late night, and maybe some vomiting, and you can wake up short on fluid. Food doesn't replace drinking water, but potatoes are roughly three-quarters water when cooked and contribute a little to the total.

## What's Actually in a Potato

Potatoes get a bad reputation because of how they're often served. The potato itself is a fairly nutritious food. Here's roughly what a medium baked potato with the skin on provides, based on standard US nutrition data (exact amounts vary with size and variety):

| Nutrient | Medium baked potato with skin (approx.) | Why it matters when hungover |
|---|---|---|
| Calories | About 160 | Real fuel without being a huge meal |
| Carbohydrate | About 35 to 37 g | Restores blood sugar and energy |
| Fiber | About 4 g (much of it in the skin) | Helps you feel full; go lighter if you have diarrhea |
| Protein | About 4 g | Modest; add eggs or yogurt for more |
| Potassium | Roughly 900 mg | One of the richest common food sources |
| Vitamin C | Roughly 15 mg | A modest contribution |
| Vitamin B6 | A meaningful share of daily needs | Part of normal energy metabolism |
| Fat | Close to zero | Easy on the stomach before you add toppings |
| Sodium | Very low | Add a pinch of salt yourself if you've lost fluid |

Two things stand out. First, a plain potato is low in fat, which is why it's gentle on the stomach. The fat comes from what you add: butter, cheese, sour cream, or the frying oil. Second, it's high in potassium and low in sodium, so if you've been sweating or vomiting, a little salt on top is actually useful rather than something to avoid.

## Potassium: The Banana Comparison and the Myth Behind It

You'll often read that potatoes beat bananas for hangovers because they have more potassium. That's true on paper. A medium baked potato carries roughly twice the potassium of a medium banana. But the premise behind it, that a hangover is mainly a potassium shortage, doesn't hold up well.

Studies that have measured electrolytes in hungover people have generally found sodium, potassium, and similar minerals close to normal, and they don't track with how bad people feel. Alcohol makes you pee more, but for a typical night out that loss isn't usually enough to leave a healthy person meaningfully low on potassium.

Where potassium really can drop is when you lose fluid in other ways: repeated vomiting, diarrhea, or very heavy, long drinking sessions. In those cases, a potassium-rich food plus fluids is a sensible combination, and a potato is a good, cheap way to get it. Our [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) guide goes deeper on the potassium myth, and the [potassium and alcohol](/never-hungover/potassium-and-alcohol) guide covers what alcohol does to potassium over time.

So the honest version is: potatoes are a good source of potassium, and that's a nice bonus, but the main reasons to eat one are the easy carbs and the gentle texture.

## Do Potatoes Absorb Alcohol?

No, not in the way people usually mean. Once alcohol is in your bloodstream, nothing you eat pulls it back out. Your liver clears it at a fairly steady pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, though this varies a lot. Eating a potato at 2 a.m. doesn't make you less drunk, and eating one in the morning doesn't speed up how quickly the rest of the alcohol leaves.

Food does matter **before and during** drinking. A meal in your stomach slows how fast alcohol moves into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That gives your liver more time to keep up and usually means a lower peak blood alcohol level. A meal with some starch, protein, and fat does this better than nothing at all. Potatoes can be part of that meal. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) covers the evidence in more detail.

The takeaway: eat before you drink, and eat after you drink because you need fuel. Don't count on any food to cancel out what you've already had.

## Mashed Potatoes for a Hangover

Mashed potatoes might be the single best potato option the morning after, especially if your stomach is delicate.

Why they work well:

- **The texture is soft and easy to swallow.** When even chewing feels like too much, mashed potatoes go down without a fight.
- **You control the fat.** A little butter or milk makes them comforting without turning them into a heavy meal. If you're very queasy, go lighter.
- **They're easy to salt.** A pinch of salt helps if you've been sweating or throwing up.
- **They're filling in small amounts.** A few spoonfuls is often enough to settle a hollow, shaky feeling.

To make them a fuller meal, stir in some plain Greek yogurt for protein, or eat them with a couple of eggs. Skip the heavy cream, piles of cheese, and garlic if your stomach is burning. If you've been vomiting, start with a few small spoonfuls after you've kept fluids down for an hour or two.

## Baked Potatoes for a Hangover

A baked potato is the most nutritious way to eat a potato, because the skin keeps a good share of the fiber and some of the minerals.

It's a good choice when your stomach feels okay and you want a real meal. A few topping ideas that help rather than hurt:

- **A little butter and salt.** Simple, comforting, and gentle.
- **Plain yogurt or cottage cheese.** Adds protein without much grease.
- **Eggs.** A baked potato with a fried or scrambled egg on top is a balanced hangover breakfast.
- **Beans.** Add protein and more fiber, though go easy if your gut is upset.

If you have diarrhea, scoop out the inside and leave most of the skin. Extra fiber can be a bit much for an irritated gut. If you're in a hurry, a potato cooks in a microwave in five to eight minutes, which beats waiting for an oven when you feel rough.

## Boiled Potatoes and Potato Soup

Boiled potatoes are the plainest option of all and a good first step back to solid food after a rough night. They're soft, mild, and easy to portion. Toss them with a little salt and olive oil or butter if you can handle it.

Potato soup is also worth a mention because it combines several things that help at once: warm liquid, salt, soft starch, and a meal that doesn't feel heavy. A simple potato and leek soup or a broth with potatoes in it gives you fluid and food in the same bowl. Very creamy, cheese-heavy versions are richer and might be too much for a sensitive stomach. Our roundup of the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover) has more options.

## French Fries, Hash Browns, and Other Fried Potatoes

This is where most people's hangover potato craving actually lands, and it deserves an honest look.

Fries and hash browns still give you the carbohydrate and salt, and they can absolutely make you feel better in the moment. Plenty of people swear by them. The downside is the fat. Fried food takes longer to leave your stomach, and on a morning when your stomach lining is already irritated, a big greasy meal can bring on more nausea, heartburn, or an urgent bathroom trip.

There's also a widespread belief that greasy food the morning after "absorbs" the alcohol. It doesn't. By the morning, most or all of the alcohol has been absorbed already. Our guide to [greasy food for a hangover](/never-hungover/greasy-food-hangover) explains why the grease cure feels good but doesn't do what people think.

A sensible middle ground:

- **If your stomach is fine,** a moderate portion of fries or hash browns with eggs and plenty of water is a reasonable choice. Enjoy it.
- **If you feel queasy,** start with something plain like toast or a few bites of mashed potato, and save the fries for later in the day.
- **If you have heartburn,** fried food is one of the more common triggers. A baked or boiled potato is the better bet. Our [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) guide covers what helps.
- **Air-fried or oven-baked potatoes** give you much of the crispy, salty appeal with far less oil.

If you're craving a full drive-through breakfast, the [best fast food for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-fast-food-for-hangover) guide compares the common options honestly.

## Potato Chips for a Hangover

Potato chips are mostly a salt craving in disguise. After a night of drinking and sweating, wanting something salty makes sense, and a handful of chips does give you some sodium and a little carbohydrate.

That's about where the benefit ends. Chips are high in fat for a small amount of food, they don't fill you up, and it's easy to eat a lot of them without getting much real fuel. They're also dry and salty, which can make you thirstier if you aren't drinking water alongside.

If chips are what you can face, they're fine as a snack with a big glass of water. Plain salted chips are easier on the stomach than spicy or vinegar flavors. A better way to scratch the same itch is a few salted crackers or pretzels, which give you salt and starch with much less fat. See our guide to [toast and crackers for a hangover](/never-hungover/toast-and-crackers-for-hangover), or the [salt for a hangover](/never-hungover/salt-for-hangover) guide if salt is the main thing you're craving.

## Sweet Potatoes for a Hangover

Sweet potatoes are a good alternative to white potatoes and work in much the same way. They provide easy carbohydrate, they're soft when cooked, and they're also a good source of potassium. They bring a lot of vitamin A (as beta-carotene, the orange pigment) and slightly more fiber.

A few practical differences:

- **They taste sweeter,** which some people find more appealing when they feel rough and others find too much.
- **They have a little more fiber,** which is good for fullness but can be harder on the gut if you have diarrhea.
- **They're easy to bake or microwave** the same way as a regular potato.

There's no good evidence that one beats the other for a hangover. Pick whichever sounds better. Mashed sweet potato with a little butter and salt is a very gentle option.

## Should You Eat Potatoes Before Drinking?

Eating a proper meal before you drink is one of the most useful things you can do, and potatoes can be part of it. A meal slows the rate at which alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which usually means a lower peak and a less punishing night.

The best pre-drinking meal tends to combine:

- **Starch** like potatoes, rice, pasta, or bread
- **Protein** like chicken, fish, eggs, beans, or tofu
- **Some fat** like olive oil, avocado, or the fat in a normal meal

A dinner of roast potatoes with chicken and vegetables, or a baked potato with chili, fits that well. A bag of chips on the way to the bar does not do the same job. It's not a meal.

To be clear about limits: eating first lowers your peak alcohol level, but it doesn't stop you from getting drunk or hungover if you drink a lot. The amount and pace of drinking still matter most.

## What If You've Been Throwing Up?

If you've been vomiting, give your stomach a break before you add food. Start with small, frequent sips of water or an oral rehydration drink. Once you've kept fluids down for an hour or two, plain starchy foods are a good first step. Boiled or mashed potatoes without much butter, plain toast, crackers, rice, or a banana are all reasonable choices.

Go slowly. A few bites, then wait. If that stays down, have a bit more. Skip fried potatoes and rich toppings until your stomach has settled. Our guide on [what to eat after throwing up from drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-after-throwing-up-from-drinking) has a step-by-step plan.

If you can't keep any fluids down for many hours, or you see blood, that's a reason to get medical care, not to keep trying foods.

## Who Should Be Careful With Potatoes

For most people, potatoes are a safe, ordinary food. A few groups should think a bit more:

- **People with kidney disease** often need to limit potassium, and potatoes are high in it. If your doctor has told you to watch potassium, follow that advice. Soaking or boiling potatoes reduces some of the potassium, but ask your care team how much is okay.
- **People taking medicines that raise potassium,** such as certain blood pressure drugs (ACE inhibitors, ARBs) or potassium-sparing diuretics, should check with their doctor or pharmacist before eating a lot of high-potassium foods.
- **People with diabetes** should remember that alcohol can lower blood sugar for many hours, and potatoes raise it fairly quickly. Monitor your glucose and follow your own care plan. Pairing potatoes with protein and fat slows the rise.
- **Anyone eating green or sprouting potatoes.** Green patches and sprouts contain more solanine, a natural compound that can cause stomach upset. Cut those parts away, or skip potatoes that are very green or taste bitter. This matters more on a morning when your stomach is already unhappy.

## A Realistic Hangover Recovery Plan (Where Potatoes Fit)

No single food fixes a hangover, but a few basic steps together make a real difference. Here's an order that works for most people:

1. **Drink water first.** Start with a glass or two, then keep sipping through the morning. If you've been vomiting or had diarrhea, an oral rehydration drink or an electrolyte mix is a better choice than plain water alone.
2. **Eat something plain once you can.** A baked or mashed potato, toast, rice, crackers, or a banana. Small amounts at first if you feel queasy.
3. **Add protein when your stomach allows.** Eggs, yogurt, or a bit of chicken. Our [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) guide explains why they pair well with starchy foods.
4. **Handle the headache carefully.** If you take a pain reliever, follow the label, take it with food, and check our guides on medication safety with alcohol before combining anything.
5. **Rest.** Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, and a nap or an early night does more for the fog than any food.
6. **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another drink just postpones the hangover.

For a broader list of what to eat, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

## Preventing the Next One

Potatoes help you recover, but the better win is waking up feeling less rough in the first place. The habits with the best evidence are not exciting: drink less, drink slower, eat a real meal before you start, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and give yourself enough sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through each one.

Some people also add a supplement. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own, and it doesn't replace eating, hydrating, or drinking less. If you'd like to try it, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple, budget-friendly option, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) is a popular combination formula. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

## The Bottom Line

- Potatoes are a good hangover food because they give you easy carbohydrate, they're gentle on the stomach, and they're rich in potassium.
- They don't absorb alcohol or lower your blood alcohol. Food helps most when you eat it before and during drinking.
- Baked, boiled, and mashed potatoes are the gentlest options. Fries, hash browns, and chips are fine if your stomach is calm, but the grease can make nausea and heartburn worse.
- Add a little salt, drink water alongside, and pair potatoes with protein like eggs when you can.
- If you've been vomiting, get fluids down first and then start with small amounts of plain potato.
- People with kidney disease or on potassium-raising medicines should check with their doctor about high-potassium foods.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Are potatoes good for a hangover?**

Yes, they're one of the better foods to eat when hungover. A plain baked, boiled, or mashed potato gives you easy carbohydrate when your blood sugar may be low, it's bland enough for a queasy stomach, and it provides a good amount of potassium. Potatoes won't cure a hangover or clear alcohol faster, but they're a solid part of a recovery meal, especially with water and some protein.

**Are mashed potatoes good for a hangover?**

Mashed potatoes are one of the gentlest options because they're soft, easy to swallow, and simple to season with a little salt. Keep the butter and cream modest if your stomach is upset, and add protein like eggs or plain yogurt to make it a fuller meal. If you've been vomiting, start with a few spoonfuls after you've kept fluids down for an hour or two.

**Are french fries good for a hangover?**

They can make you feel better in the moment because they give you starch and salt, but the frying oil makes them harder on an irritated stomach. If your stomach feels fine, a moderate portion with water and some protein is reasonable. If you're nauseous or have heartburn, a baked or mashed potato is the better choice. Fries don't absorb alcohol that's already in your blood.

**Do potatoes absorb alcohol?**

No. Once alcohol is in your bloodstream, no food pulls it back out, and your liver clears it at its own pace. Eating before and during drinking does slow how fast alcohol is absorbed, which usually lowers your peak blood alcohol level. That's why a meal with potatoes before you go out helps more than potatoes the next morning.

**Do potatoes have more potassium than bananas?**

Yes. A medium baked potato with the skin has roughly twice the potassium of a medium banana. That's useful if you've lost fluid from vomiting or diarrhea. Keep in mind that most people with an ordinary hangover aren't seriously low on potassium, so the bigger benefits of a potato are the easy carbs and gentle texture.

**Are potato chips good for a hangover?**

Not especially. Chips satisfy a salt craving and give you a little carbohydrate, but they're high in fat for the amount of food and don't fill you up. If chips are what you can manage, eat them with plenty of water. Salted crackers, pretzels, or a lightly salted baked potato give you the same salt and starch with much less grease.

**Is a sweet potato or a regular potato better for a hangover?**

There's no good evidence that one is better than the other. Both provide easy carbohydrate and potassium and are gentle when baked or mashed. Sweet potatoes add vitamin A and a little more fiber, which may be harder on your gut if you have diarrhea. Choose whichever sounds more appealing.

**Should I eat potatoes before drinking?**

A real meal before drinking is one of the most useful things you can do, and potatoes make a good part of it. Pair them with protein and some fat, such as chicken and roast potatoes or a baked potato with chili. Food slows alcohol absorption and lowers your peak blood alcohol level, though it won't stop you from getting drunk or hungover if you drink a lot.
